steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and parts for transit damage; report anything damaged or missing to the dealer. Remove any packaging from the flue collar before installing the chimney.

A separate box underneath the stove holds some of the internal parts, with an instruction sheet for installing them.

Pack listStove, stone kit A, stone kit B, owner's manual

The label is attached by a cable to the bottom of the stove. Don't damage the label or cable when lifting; after final positioning, store the label in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
Choose the location
Freestanding room heater only: never in a fireplace or factory-built fireplace. Main living area, near the chimney, away from traffic, doors and hallways, and never near stored flammable liquids.

Confirm the stove and stovepipe will have the required clearances to every combustible: walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase.

Clearances can be reduced with an NFPA-approved wall protection system (NFPA Code 211), with the approval of the authority having jurisdiction.

The manual's diagrams show typical installations and are specific to Simpson Dura-Vent DVL. A rear connector pipe must be UL listed; check its listing for the correct clearances.
Floor protection
On a combustible floor, a noncombustible floor protector goes under the stove and beyond it: minimum 38in x 36-1/2in (US) or 45-1/2in x 46-1/4in (Canada). No insulated hearth pad or R-value needed.

Example: a hearth with a continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass, steel or another noncombustible facing. How far it must extend beyond the stove is shown in the hearth dimensions diagram on p. 9.

Compliant to CAN/ULC-S627 installation directly over a combustible floor with proper ember protection; radiant floor insulation protection is not required.

Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring maker's temperature limit; extra shielding may be needed.
Set clearances

Position the stove per the clearance tables: top exit (p. 10), alcove (p. 11), rear exit (p. 12). A rear heatshield (kit 5968-011) reduces the listed clearances; minimum unprotected ceiling height for vertical exit is 92-3/8".
Wall pass-through
The connector may not pass through a floor, ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or concealed space. Through a combustible wall, the installation must conform to NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA-B365.

The four wall pass-through systems the manual lists:

  • A. Minimum 3.5in thick brick masonry framed into the combustible wall, with a minimum 12in of brick from clay liner to combustibles. The fire clay liner runs from the outer surface of the brick wall to, but not beyond, the inner surface of the chimney flue liner, firmly cemented.
  • B. Solid-insulated, listed factory-built chimney length of the same inside diameter as the connector, with 1in or more of insulation and a minimum 9in air space to combustibles.
  • C. Sheet steel connector, minimum 24 gauge, with a ventilated thimble (minimum 24 gauge, two 1in air channels), separated from combustibles by a minimum of 6in of glass fiber insulation. Opening covered, thimble supported with minimum 24 gauge sheet steel.
  • D. Solid insulated, listed factory-built chimney length with an inside diameter 2in larger than the connector and 1in or more of insulation, as a pass-through for a minimum 24 gauge single wall connector, with a minimum 2in air space to combustibles. Chimney section at least 12in long, spaced 1in from the connector with sheet steel support plates at both ends; fasteners must not penetrate the chimney flue liner.
Outside air (optional)
Kit 96-53400 connects the stove's air intake to a minimum 3" duct to outdoors (duct by others). Terminate at or below the stove's air intake, screened and hooded. Required in mobile homes.
Chimney connector

6" 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel single wall, or listed double wall; no aluminum or galvanized pipe. Crimped ends toward the stove, three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws at every joint including the flue collar; horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

• Keep the stove as close to the chimney as practical and the stovepipe as short and straight as possible. Extra length or elbows add draft resistance and creosote.
  • Double wall connector (with a listed Type HT chimney or a masonry chimney, to reduce clearances): for example Simpson Dura Vent DVL or Metalbestos DS. The manual's double wall clearances are specific to DVL.
  • Telescoping pipes, slip-connectors and clean-out tees ease inspection and let you dismantle the stovepipe without moving the stove.
  • Never connect to a chimney flue used by another appliance, or to any air distribution duct or system. Don't use stovepipe as a chimney.
  • Maintain the vapor barrier where the chimney or other component penetrates the exterior.
Connect to the chimney

Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner; 6" inside diameter for new installations. Have a professional examine a masonry chimney first and finish any repairs.

The chimney may not be smaller than the flue collar, or more than three times its cross-sectional area. Choose an interior chimney when possible: it heats quickly, drafts better and discourages creosote.

Prefabricated metal chimney

Follow the maker's instructions precisely. Buy the wall pass-through (or ceiling support package), "T" section, fire-stops, insulation shield, roof flashing and chimney cap from the same maker.

Masonry chimney

  • Mortared brick or modular block at least 4" thick, or a mortared rubble or stone wall: both must use a liner.
  • Liners: tile (minimum 5/8" wall, refractory mortar, at least 1" air space), UL listed 6" stainless steel (insulated, wrapped or surrounded with vermiculite), or another listed Type HT liner system. A liner shall be rated to UL 1777 or ULC S635.
  • The cleanout door must close completely and seal tight.
  • Interior chimney: at least 2" clearance to combustibles, fire stops at floors and ceilings, insulation at least 2" away. Exterior chimney: at least 1" clearance.
Note: p. 7 gives the square masonry flue size as 7" x 7" (square flue); p. 16 says to use a maximum 6" x 6" tile size for best results.
Chimney height & draft

Minimum chimney height: 16 feet off the floor for top exit, 19 feet for rear exit; recommended maximum 30 feet. Check the draft at installation: it must be between 0.06" and 0.1" WC; above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper.

• Top exit: 16 feet (4.9 m) off the floor or 13 feet 5 inches (4.1 m) from the top of the stove.
  • Rear exit: 19 feet (5.8m) off the floor or 16 feet 5 inches (5.0m) from the top of the stove.
  • At least 3 feet higher than the highest part of the roof opening it passes through, and at least 2 feet higher than any part of the roof within 10 feet measured horizontally.
  • A tall chimney can over-draft; some installations need more than one damper.
Mobile home installs

Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD): outside air kit, stove permanently attached to the floor with the shipping clips, and a listed mobile home chimney and connector kit with spark arrester. Never in a sleeping room.

• The Mobile Home Chimney and Connector Kit (to UL103 or CAN/ULC-S629) must include a stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, and a 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove, at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes through and at least 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet.
  • Roof terminations must be removable and re-installable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools; mechanically secure the chimney to the ceiling support box.
  • A chimney that exits other than through the roof, at 7 feet or less above ground, needs a guard at the exit up to 7 feet.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof. Remove the chimney when transporting the home.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Door opened cold → fully open the primary air one minute first; open the bypass before the door
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Blocked chimney → examine chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized / undersized / too-short chimney → reline / draft inducer or replace / lengthen
Air leaking into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed or catalysts not working → close it in the active range; brush, vacuum or replace the catalysts
Another appliance on the flue → disconnect it and seal the openings

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets; replace a leaking glass gasket
Excessive draft → operate at low burn; over 0.1 wc needs stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long chimney → shorten it or install stovepipe damper(s)
Oversized chimney → reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Check first: a 400° F stovepipe, measured no more than 12 inches above the flue collar, means the stove is supplying enough heat
Poor-quality, low-Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, preferably dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate it
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → check the installation; insulated prefab or properly sized masonry chimney
Excessive ash build-up → empty the ashes more often

panels.title: Catalyst problems
items: Fly ash build-up (light-off not maintained, bypass closed too soon) → brush the cold combustor or vacuum lightly; follow the light-off procedure
Char and fly ash from cardboard, gift wrap or garbage → burn only dry, seasoned wood
Plugging with soot or creosote (wet or pitchy wood, small-diameter loads) → hot fire with the bypass open until well in the operating range, then run hot for one hour
Warping or bowing (too hot for long periods) → reduce the air setting to keep catalysts in the operating range

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build the fire right on the firebox floor; don't use a grate. You'll use the bypass handle and the primary air lever (under the ash lip).

  1. Open the bypass (handle pointing toward the front). Open the door and put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Build a tee-pee of about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long, over the paper.
  2. Pull the primary air lever all the way out.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling burns and the draft starts to pull.
  4. Close the door and let the fire burn.
  5. Once the kindling is going, add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass.
  6. When the catalyst thermometer reads in the Active range, close the bypass.
  7. Let the stove run on high for about 20 minutes.
  8. Then set the burn rate with the primary air lever.

Reloading

Open the bypass before you open the door. Open the door just a crack, pause, then open it fully so smoke can clear. Reload on a bed of hot, red coals, and keep big coals off the ash lip so the door seals.

Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Keep the door closed while the stove is burning.

breakin.title: Breaking in your stove
breakin.html:
Your stove's soapstone holds natural moisture that must be driven out slowly. Over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone or damage other parts. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, like this:

  1. Open the bypass. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" thick, 10" to 16" long) crisscrossed on top.
  2. Pull the primary air control fully open, toward you.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches and the draft pulls.
  4. Close the door. Keep a steady, low-heat fire: the stove should feel warm, not hot. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once the stove is warm, push the air control fully in and let the fire die out. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing mean the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smell are normal at first

The first fires give off some smoke and fumes as the paints and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. If an odor persists, contact your dealer. These cool fires can build creosote fast, so check the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is done.

bypass.title: The bypass and catalyst thermometer
bypass.html:
The bypass handle sends smoke either around the catalytic combustor (open) or through it (closed). The combustor's catalysts burn up smoke, so the stove runs cleanest with the bypass closed and the catalysts hot.

Handle toward the frontBypass open
Handle toward the rearBypass closed

Follow the thermometer

  • Inactive: keep the bypass open until the stove heats up.
  • Active: close the bypass, and keep it closed while the stove burns in this range.
  • Too Hot: keep the door closed, close the air control fully and let the stove cool back into the Active range.

The stove typically runs at 800 °F to 1300 °F. The thermometer reads best pulled out 3/8" from the stove body.

Always open the bypass before you open the door. After reloading a cool fire, or one burned down to charcoal, run it at medium to high for about 10 minutes so the catalysts reach about 600 °F, then close the bypass.

air.title: Air control and burn rates
air.html:
The primary air lever sits under the ash lip. Pull it out for more air and a hotter, faster fire; push it in for a slower, cooler one. It never closes completely, by design.

LowLever all the way in
Medium-lowFrom low, pull out a little less than 1/4"
Medium-highFrom low, pull out a little less than 1/2"
HighLever all the way out

Medium-low is the typical setting and the best one when you leave the stove unattended. Long stretches on low can build creosote, so run the stove on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.

Signs of over-firing

Never over-fire your stove. It damages the stove. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe. Too much draft, the wrong fuel, worn gaskets or an open door can cause it. If you suspect over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer. Over-firing damage isn't covered, and any sign of it voids the warranty.

The minimum burn rate is set at the factory. It's against federal regulations to change it.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). Hardwoods burn longer and make better coals; softwoods burn hotter and faster. Dryness matters most: green wood may give less than 2000 Btu per pound, dry wood up to 7000.

Season it

  • Split, stack and air-dry green wood for a year.
  • Seasoned firewood is typically at or below 20% moisture. A hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Stack it on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Don't store firewood inside the stove's clearances.

Never burn

Coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, garbage or trash, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), plywood or particleboard, painted, treated (including pressure treated) or kiln-dried wood, unseasoned (green) wood, paints or paint thinners, solvents, waste petroleum products, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, lawn clippings, manure or animal remains, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt water saturated materials, flammable fluids, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, anything containing plastic or rubber (including tires), or anything other than natural cordwood. These can damage the catalysts, give off toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective and cause smoke, or cause dangerous burning. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

The manual includes a table ranking common species by heat content per cord.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Only clean the glass when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. For the inside, dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the glass in circles.
  2. Once the deposits are gone, finish with window cleaner or a stove-glass cleaner from your dealer. Use the same on the outside.
  3. Wipe the cleaner off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
No razor blades, steel wool or other abrasives. Scratches and etching weaken the glass. Use only cleaners made for wood stoves.

Glass that won't stay clean

If the glass is always dirty, the stove is running too cool or the wood is wet, which also means more creosote. A good hot fire cleans it: about 20 minutes on high after you close the bypass burns off residue from low fires. Keeping logs away from the glass lets the air-wash do its job.

The glass is a tough ceramic rated to 2300° F, but don't strike or slam the door, and don't use the stove with cracked or broken glass. Replacement glass (kit 96-58805) comes from your dealer.

ash.title: Removing the ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox if you like.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Use a fireplace shovel. Push large live coals to the side and take only the finer ash.
  3. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in it, and don't pour water in.
  4. Close the lid and take the container outside right away. Set it on a noncombustible surface or the ground, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles.
  5. Keep the ashes in the closed container until all the coals are thoroughly cool.
Coals in ashes can stay hot for several days. Never use wooden or plastic containers, paper or plastic bags, or a trash can, and never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.

Don't let ashes build up around the door opening. They spill out and can pack into the gasket channel so the door won't seal.

care.title: Care and creosote checks
care.html:
The manual's routine for keeping the stove and chimney safe:

Every day at first

  • Check for creosote daily until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe.

Every week

  • Empty the ashes, sooner if the firebox is full.

Every other month

  • Check the chimney connector and chimney for creosote, the tar-like deposit that fuels chimney fires. Remove it if more than 1/8" has built up, and check at least monthly while it's building.
  • Dollar-bill test: on a cool stove, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the door latch or replace the door gasket.
  • Brush fly ash or soot off the face of the catalytic combustor with a soft-bristled brush.

End of every season

  • Take apart and clean the chimney connector; replace pieces that show rust or wear.
  • Inspect and, if needed, clean the chimney. Clean out the stove.
  • Check and clean the catalytic combustor if needed.
  • Replace door gasket that's worn, frayed, cracked or very hard. Plan on new gasket every two to three seasons.
Before each heating season, have the whole system professionally inspected and cleaned. A certified chimney sweep is recommended.

safety.title: Safety and chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a stovepipe or chimney fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away. If not:
  2. Close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass.
  5. Keep the front door closed.

When the chimney fire is out, leave the air control and bypass closed and let the fire in the stove die out completely. Inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney for damage, and fix any damage before you use the stove again.

Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney to put out a chimney fire. The extreme heat turns it to steam instantly and can cause serious injury.

Every day

  • The stove is hot when it's burning. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away.
  • Keep furniture, drapes and other combustibles at least 36" from the stove.
  • Install smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors throughout your home, including bedrooms and hallways, and test them.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher rated "A B C" handy.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's warranty covers the original purchaser only and isn't transferable. It starts on the original invoice date and covers a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Appliance electrical and gas components2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, all components not listed elsewhere1 year

A few lines of the coverage grid (air supply system, refractory, baffles) are marked by fuel type; check those on page 38. Hearthstone pays dealer labor in the first year and parts shipping in the first 90 days.

Catalysts

Covered by their maker, Applied Ceramics: free replacement within two (2) years, then $130.00 in year 3, $140.00 in year 4, $150.00 in year 5 and $160.00 in year 6.

Note: the catalyst warranty gives the free-replacement period as two (2) years, then refers to "the three year period" when it promises one replacement catalyst for each defective catalyst returned (p. 37).

Not covered

Over-firing, fuels the manual doesn't list, installation or use not per the manual, and normal wear on parts like paint, gaskets, baffles, refractory and glass. Claims go through your dealer; registration isn't required for coverage.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
US minimum38in x 36-1/2in
Canada minimum45-1/2in x 46-1/4in
InsulationNo insulated hearth pad; no R-value requirement

A noncombustible floor protector is required between a combustible floor and the stove, under the stove and extending beyond it. How far it extends on each side is shown in the hearth dimensions diagram on this page.

Compliant to CAN/ULC-S627 installation directly over a combustible floor, with proper ember protection. Radiant floor insulation protection is not required.

Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Consult the flooring maker; additional shielding may be necessary.

specAir.title: Outside air supply
specAir.html:
The optional outside air kit #96-53400 attaches to the underside of the stove and connects its air intake to a minimum 3" (76 mm) diameter duct to the outside (supplied by others). An adaptor for 4" duct is available: kit #90-53308.

  • The IRC does not allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance. Hearthstone recommends terminating at the same level as, or lower than, the stove's air intake.
  • Locate the termination where snow, leaves or other material can't block it. Screen it with ¼" x ¼" mesh rodent screen and cover it with a rain/wind proof hood (supplied by others).
  • Canada: install a damper allowing 100% closure, and attach the stove to the floor with the shipping clips and fasteners long enough to reach the subfloor.
  • Mobile homes: an outside air kit must be used.

Outside air may be required if the stove doesn't draw steadily, smoke rolls out or it back-drafts; if other fuel-fired equipment smells or back-drafts; if opening a window slightly on a calm day helps; if the house is tightly sealed or has powered exhaust; with excessive winter window condensation; or with a ventilation system.

conflicts.issue: Square masonry flue size: specifications give 7" x 7" (178 x 178 mm) square flue; the masonry chimney section says use a maximum 6" diameter or 6" x 6" tile size for best results. Also shown in step7.

Canadian single-wall connector with rear heat shield: the "Canadian Req. Only" row gives B 15-1/2" / C 21" (p. 10), but the alcove single-wall-with-heat-shield row in the same Canadian table gives B 5-1/2" / C 11", and the rear-exit table gives 5-1/2" back wall to top casting (8" to pipe edge) for Canada with a rear shield (p. 12).

Catalyst (Applied Ceramics) warranty: no-charge replacement "with two (2) years", prorated from Year 3, but the same text then says one replacement catalyst per defective catalyst returned "during the three year period".

review.notes: Emission rate is printed '0.53 gr/hr.' on p. 2 and '0.53 g/hr.' on p. 7; read 'gr' as grams (EPA standard units) and used g/hr, not flagged as a conflict. Burn time is printed 'Over to 24 hrs. (Heat Life: Up to 30 hours)' on p. 7, apparently a typo for 'Up to'; the guide quotes it rather than rewording. Clearance letters A-F on p. 10 are defined only in the drawing (Figure 4); the guide lists the table values by letter and does not assign them to sides/rear/corner. Trim and mantel clearances (p. 11) and the floor-protector extension on each side (p. 9) exist only in diagrams and were not transcribed. Acceptable catalyst distortion range is only in Figure 20 (p. 29). The p. 12 rear-exit table headers are scrambled in the layout text; the raw page text confirms four columns: With Rear Shield US*, With Rear Shield CANADA*, No Rear Heat Shield US, No Rear Heat Shield CANADA. Warranty grid (p. 38) is a check-mark table: only rows marked for all three fuels were listed; rows with one or two marks (clean burning air supply system; refractory, vermiculite panels, baffles; burner and logs; burn pot and baffles; ash grate) were not assigned to wood. Canadian clearance table is headed 'ULCS 628' (p. 10) while the cover and pp. 8-9 cite ULC S627 (S627-2023 on the cover). Manual cross-references are off: figure numbers 4, 5 and 6 are each used twice; p. 10 sends rear-exit readers to 'Figure 5, on page 11' (actually Figure 6, p. 12); p. 17 says 'SEE FIGURE 8' for chimney height (Figure 5 on p. 17); p. 26 low burn says '(See figure 13)' (the thermometer); p. 5 says over-firing 'See page 24' (caution is on p. 26). The guide cites pages, not figure numbers. Kindling metric conversion differs (16" = 457 mm on p. 24, 406 mm on p. 25); the guide uses inches only. Emergency procedure (p. 6) says 'perform the next three steps' but lists four; all four are given. The 4" duct adaptor kit number is split across two lines on p. 14 ('KIT #90-' / '53308'). The manual lists a blower kit (96-57801) as optional but gives no blower operating instructions, so there is no blower tile.
